opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea was to take the structure that already works well in a real research lab and translate it into a team of AI agents. In my own lab at Stanford, there's a PI who sets the overall direction, and then there are students and postdocs with different expertise. Some are more on the biology side, some on machine learning, some on computational methods. We have group meetings where everyone discusses the big picture, and then a lot of one-on-one meetings where someone goes deep on a specific task.

The Virtual Lab mirrors that pretty directly. There's an AI PI agent, which is a language model prompted to act as the lab lead. The human researcher, which in our case was me and my collaborators, gives the PI agent a high-level research goal. In our main project, that goal was designing new nanobodies that could bind to recent variants of SARS-CoV-2.

The PI agent then decides what expertise the team needs and creates its own scientist agents. For the nanobody project, it created an immunologist agent, a computational biologist agent, and a machine learning specialist agent. Each one has a defined role, expertise, and goal.

We also added a scientific critic agent. That turned out to be really important. Its job is to poke holes in the proposals, ask whether claims are justified, and point out errors or vague reasoning. Language models can be overly agreeable, so having one agent whose explicit role is to be skeptical improved the quality of the discussion a lot.

Then there are two kinds of meetings, just like in a real lab. In team meetings, the PI poses an agenda, each scientist agent contributes over several rounds, the critic gives feedback, and the PI synthesizes everything into a decision. That's where the big strategic questions get decided, like whether to design antibodies or nanobodies, and whether to start from scratch or modify existing nanobodies. In individual meetings, a single agent works on a concrete task, like writing code for a particular tool, often with the critic reviewing it.

In terms of the human role, we tried to keep it fairly light. The human sets the agenda and gives occasional high-level guidance, but most of the discussion and decision-making happens among the agents. In our nanobody project, the human contribution was only a small fraction of the total words exchanged.

The agents ended up designing a computational pipeline using tools like ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta, and that pipeline produced nanobody designs. When we tested them in the wet lab, several showed good expression, and a couple of them showed improved binding to newer variants while retaining binding to the original strain. So the Virtual Lab structure didn't just produce interesting conversations. It led to real experimental results.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI PI synthesizes the agents’ team-meeting contributions into a decision, but it does not say that decision is a consensus solution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the whole idea of the Virtual Lab really came from looking at how my own group at Stanford actually operates day to day. If you think about how a physical lab works, it's not one person doing everything. I'm the PI, I set the direction, I pick the problems, but I'm certainly not the person doing the structural biology or the machine learning or the immunology at the bench. We have students and postdocs who each bring deep expertise in one area, and the science happens in the interactions between them.

So we tried to mirror that structure almost literally. There's a principal investigator agent, which is an LLM playing the role of the PI. Its job is to think about what the project needs, and then it actually creates the team. It decides, okay, for this problem we need an immunologist, we need a computational biologist, we need someone who knows machine learning. Each of those becomes its own agent with its own persona and its own area of expertise. And then there's a critic agent whose entire role is to be skeptical, to push back, to point out when the reasoning is sloppy or an assumption doesn't hold. That's something you see in good labs too, that one person who always asks the hard question in group meeting.

And then the way the work actually gets done also looks like a real lab. We have team meetings, where the PI poses a question, every agent weighs in from their perspective, the critic responds, and they go back and forth over several rounds until they converge on a decision. And then we have individual meetings, which are more like the one-on-one between an advisor and a student, where a single agent goes off and does a focused piece of work, like writing code to run a particular analysis, and brings it back.

The human, in this case me and my collaborators, sit at a level above all of that. We're not scripting every step. We give high-level guidance, we set the agenda for a meeting, we review the outputs, and we intervene when something is going sideways. It's honestly a lot like what I do with my actual lab, which is mostly asking questions and steering rather than executing.

One thing that surprised us is how much the structure matters. If you just ask a single model to design nanobodies for a new COVID variant, you get something fairly generic. But when you have the computational biologist agent arguing with the immunologist agent, and the critic saying your evaluation metric doesn't make sense, the quality of the resulting plan goes up a lot. The division of labor and the disagreement are doing real work, which is exactly what you'd hope, because that's why physical labs are organized this way in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says the PI agent poses questions and the agents discuss them over several rounds until they converge on a decision, but it does not say the AI professor synthesizes their contributions into the consensus solution.

astra-6.text:
The way we structure the Virtual Lab is to have an AI principal investigator, or PI, working with a team of AI scientists. The PI helps define the research direction, breaks the problem into smaller tasks, and brings together scientists with the expertise needed for the project. That’s similar to how I work with people in my own lab: we have a shared goal, but different people contribute different perspectives and skills.

Then we organize the work around meetings. In a team meeting, the scientists discuss ideas, critique one another’s proposals, and decide on a direction. In individual meetings, a scientist can work on a more specific question and bring the results back to the group. That lets us alternate between broad discussion and focused work.

The human researcher provides the overarching question and feedback at key points. So the idea is to give the AI team room to develop and challenge ideas while keeping the research grounded in a goal that the human cares about.

r001.rationale: The response says the scientists discuss and critique ideas and decide on a direction, but does not state that the AI PI synthesizes their contributions into a consensus solution to the research questions.

sol-6.1.text:
We structure the Virtual Lab around a team of AI scientists, rather than asking a single model to do everything. There’s an AI principal investigator who helps define the research agenda and coordinates the work, and then there are specialist agents with expertise relevant to the project—for example, in biology, machine learning, or computational chemistry.

The interaction is organized around meetings, much like in my physical lab. In a team meeting, the scientists discuss the problem, propose approaches, and critique one another’s ideas. Then individual scientists can go off and work on specific tasks and bring their results back to the group. We also include a scientific critic whose role is to challenge assumptions and identify weaknesses.

The human researcher provides the overall direction and feedback at key points. So the idea is to capture that iterative process of discussion, independent work, and revision that makes a research team productive.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI principal investigator defines the agenda and coordinates work, while scientists discuss and critique ideas. It does not state that the AI professor synthesizes those contributions into a consensus solution.
